articles.title: How to turn a PDF or Word file into Markdown for AI and notes
articles.excerpt: You want the text out of a PDF, a Word file, or a web page — with the headings and tables still looking like headings and tables. Then you can paste it into a notes app, or cut it into chunks for AI s…
articles.body: You want the text out of a PDF, a Word file, or a web page — with the headings and tables still looking like headings and tables. Then you can paste it into a notes app, or cut it into chunks for AI search (RAG). Copy and paste from a PDF often breaks this. Headings vanish. Tables become a pile of words. Words split at the end of a line stay split. This page shows a better path, starting with a free local tool. What "clean Markdown" means here Good output looks like this: Headings use # , ## , ### Tables are real Markdown tables, not a jumble Lists stay as lists A hyphen at the end of a line is joined back to the next word For AI search, each chunk can keep its heading path and page numbers Free local tool: doc2md-lite doc2md-lite is a free tool you run on your own computer.
articles.author: Tidy Byte Tools

articles.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro vs Claude Opus 5.5 for coding agents
articles.excerpt: Originally published on the QuickSilver Pro blog. Kimi K3.1 Pro is Moonshot's flagship model, and the usual comparison for it is Claude Opus 5.5. Most of those comparisons quote benchmark scores. We w…
articles.body: Originally published on the QuickSilver Pro blog . Kimi K3.1 Pro is Moonshot's flagship model, and the usual comparison for it is Claude Opus 5.5. Most of those comparisons quote benchmark scores. We wanted to know what happens when you put both into the same coding agent and give them the same tasks: do they finish, how long do they take, and what does a task cost? On QuickSilver Pro, Kimi K3.1 Pro costs $2.00 / $10.00 per million tokens and Claude Opus 5.5 costs $1.00 / $5.00. Here Kimi is the more expensive of the two per token. Short answer, from 24 runs: Quality: a tie. Both models passed every hidden test in every run. Time: 409 seconds per task on average for Kimi K3.1 Pro, against 82 for Opus 5.5. Kimi took 4 to 6.6 times as long on every task.

articles.body: Update: the Node.js build of OpenCode for older CPUs is now on v2.2.7 . If you missed the first post: the official Windows binary is compiled with Bun, and Bun refuses to start on CPUs without SSE4.2: this CPU is missing SSE4.2 support, which Bun requires This build packages OpenCode as a Node.js executable, so that check never runs. Nothing to install, just extract and run. Repo: https://github.com/foxauraai/opencode-node/ What changed Rebuilt from the official v2.2.7 tag (commit fedc6f2 ) Upgrade Remove any old version and cache first Download the new zip from the Releases page. Extract it to a new folder, for example C:\opencode-2.2.7 . Run: cd / d C : \ opencode - 2.2 . 7 \ cli - node - windows - x64 OpenCode .

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 10, 2013: Europe's GOCE satellite, the 'Ferrari of space,' fell out of orbit after mapping Earth's gravity field
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 10, 2013, Europe's GOCE satellite fell to Earth after four years in orbit mapping the planet's gravitational field. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 10, 2013, Europe's GOCE satellite fell to Earth after four years in orbit mapping the planet's gravitational field. GOCE, its name was short for Gravity field and steady-state Ocean Circulation Explorer, launched in 2009 on a mission to map Earth's gravity like never before. But despite that successful mission, it was doomed in 2013 when it ran out of fuel . At the time, controllers weren't sure where GOCE would fall back to Earth . Some people worried that it might crash into a populated area. However, the small spacecraft broke up in the atmosphere and didn't cause any property damage. It disintegrated about 50 miles above the Falkland Islands in the South Atlantic Ocean. The European Space Agency called the mission a success. GOCE lasted far longer than expected.

articles.title: A distant exoplanet mysteriously vanished from sight. Astronomers just discovered why
articles.excerpt: Astronomers have solved the mystery of an exoplanet that "disappeared" after seven years of observations.
articles.body: Astronomers have solved the mystery of an extrasolar planet, or exoplanet, that "disappeared" after seven years of observations. New research suggests that the planet hasn't vanished at all, but has been dragged off its orbit by an unseen planet. The exoplanet , designated TOI-2535 b, is located around 1,000 light-years away. TOI-2535 b was routinely observed with NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite ( TESS ) space telescope for seven years between April 2019 and March 2026 as it completed its 8.25-Earth day orbit of its parent star. That's 10 times quicker than the orbit of Mercury around the sun and means this blisteringly hot planet is classed as a " hot Jupiter ." However, something strange happened started to happen as astronomers observed the distant world.
